narratives.narrative: Psa 7:17 closes a psalm of pursued innocence with thanks. The sense is 'give thanks and sing' (101), typed as affect (102): felt gratitude, not merely a duty performed. No interior source is traced (103 absent) and no bodily organ is named as its seat (104=none) - thanksgiving here is not lodged in an organ but is a posture of the whole inner self. The bearer is the psalmist (105); the operation (106) is the whole movement of the psalm landing: vindication sought throughout is answered with praise, thanks to the LORD 'due to his righteousness' and song to his name. Its target is thanksgiving itself (107) - the interior's own grateful discharge - and it is coupled to song, 'thanks-and-sing' (112). Manner is none (108), and intensity, specifier, and effect are all unrecorded (109-111): the thanks is logged as an endpoint, ungraded and without a further consequence - it terminates in itself. Nothing is prohibited (113). The discovery note (114) shows the interior already praising before rescue is visibly complete: the righteous judge is trusted, so the self rests in gratitude. Typed as a characteristic (115) and located internally as an inner-being state (116), this is thanksgiving as the resting-place the inner life reaches when it entrusts its cause to a just God.
narratives.story: This psalm is the cry of a man being hunted, protesting his innocence and begging a righteous God to judge his case. It ends not in relief but in gratitude and song - he thanks the LORD for his righteousness and sings to his name. The thankfulness is a felt thing, welling up from the whole person rather than from any one part of him, and it needs no separate cause: trusting that his judge is just, the man is already grateful before the rescue is even complete. The gratitude does not lead anywhere further; it is where his inner life comes to rest, blending seamlessly into praise.
narratives.variation_note: Distinct among the 'thank' readings as an inner landing-point: typed as affect with an internal locus (an ib-state), where the whole psalm's movement resolves into felt gratitude twinned with song - unlike the public-vow (35:18) or the summons-refrains of Ps 107.

narratives.narrative: Psa 9:1 opens with resolve: 'I will give thanks to the LORD with my whole heart.' The sense is 'give thanks with whole heart' (101), typed as affect (102) - gratitude felt and owned. No prior interior source is named (103 absent): the thanks is presented as the self's own undivided resolve rather than a traced cause. No organ is its seat (104=none), yet the whole heart is invoked in the sense and operation - meaning not a located organ but the entire inner self given over. The bearer is the psalmist (105); the operation (106) is the self resolving to thank the LORD wholeheartedly while recounting all his wonders - undivided gratitude with nothing held back. Its target is wholehearted-thanks (107) and it is coupled as 'thank-whole-heart' (112). Manner is none (108); intensity, specifier, effect all unrecorded (109-111) - the thanks is an endpoint, not a means to a further result. Nothing is prohibited (113). The discovery (114) stresses the interior giving itself entire. Typed as a characteristic (115), located internally as an ib-state (116): here thanksgiving is the whole inner life converging, without reservation, on gratitude.
narratives.story: The psalmist begins by pledging to thank God with his whole heart and to tell of every wonderful thing God has done. What stands out is the completeness of it - not a corner of him is held back. The gratitude is a felt devotion that rises straight from him, needing no argument to justify it. It is not aimed at producing anything else; giving thanks is itself the thing his entire inner life is bent on doing.
narratives.variation_note: Marked off from the other 'give thanks' readings by its wholeheartedness and internal locus: gratitude typed as affect that gathers the entire inner self, an ib-state rather than the God-directed public act that dominates this item elsewhere (e.g. 57:9; 118:1).

narratives.narrative: Psa 35:18 turns an appeal for rescue into a pledge of public praise: 'I will thank you in the great congregation.' Its sense carries the whole clause (101), and it is typed as volition (102) - a vow of the will, not yet a discharged act. No interior source is traced (103 absent) and no organ seats it (104=none): the thanks is a resolve of the whole self, not organ-lodged. The bearer is the psalmist (105); the operation (106) is the self vowing to thank God in the great congregation, to praise him among the mighty throng - gratitude aimed at public discharge. Its target is public-thanks (107), coupled as 'thank-in-congregation' (112). Manner is none (108); intensity, specifier, effect unrecorded (109-111) - the vow is registered without gradation or downstream result. Nothing is prohibited (113). The discovery (114) shows the operation converting an anticipated rescue into a pledge of public thanksgiving. Typed as a characteristic (115), located internally as an ib-state (116): the inner life, still awaiting rescue, already binds itself by a vow of open, communal gratitude.
narratives.story: In the middle of pleading to be saved from those who hate him, the psalmist stops and makes a promise: when he is delivered he will thank God out loud, in the great assembly, before the whole crowd. The thanks here is a decision of the will more than a feeling yet realised - a vow made in advance. It rises from the whole man rather than any single faculty, and it is pointed outward toward a public setting. Even before the rescue arrives, his inner life has committed itself to grateful praise in front of everyone.
narratives.variation_note: Unusual among 'thank' readings as a willed vow (typed volition, not affect or action) with an internal locus: gratitude pledged toward a future public congregation while still awaiting rescue - distinct from the already-landed affect of 7:17 and the summons-refrains of Ps 107.

narratives.narrative: Psa 44:8 sets a settled national gratitude before the psalm's bitter turn: 'in God we have boasted... and we will give thanks to your name forever.' The sense is yadah, give thanks (101), typed as action (102). No interior source is traced (103 absent) and no organ seats it (104=none). The bearer is not an individual but the nation (105) - corporate gratitude. The operation (106) is simply to give thanks; its target is 'your name' (107), and its manner is 'forever' (108), an unbounded duration. Intensity, specifier, effect are unrecorded (109-111): the thanks is an endpoint without logged gradation or consequence. The coupling (112) is a pair with boasting (278852->278850) - thanksgiving welded to the nation's glorying in God. Nothing is prohibited (113). The discovery (114) names it the vow of perpetual praise joined to boasting, the people's settled devotion standing just before the lament breaks. Typed as a characteristic (115), its locus is God-ward (116 external:god): the movement is oriented outside the self, toward God's name. Here the inner life of a whole community expresses gratitude as its lasting boast - and the psalm will let that confident thanks collide with unexplained defeat.
narratives.story: Here a whole nation speaks, remembering how God won them the land and declaring that in him they have always boasted and will thank his name forever. The thanks is a corporate act, an enduring devotion with no end-date, tightly bound to their proud confidence in God. It is aimed squarely outward at God himself. What makes the moment sharp is its placement: this settled, forever gratitude stands right before the psalm turns to protest defeat and abandonment - the confident thanks is about to be tested against bitter experience.
narratives.variation_note: Distinct within 'give thanks' by its bearer - the nation, not the psalmist - and its coupling to boasting: corporate, God-directed, 'forever' gratitude set just before a lament's turn, unlike the individual wholehearted thanks of 9:1 or 111:1.

narratives.narrative: Psa 50:14 reframes worship itself: 'Offer to God a sacrifice of thanksgiving.' The sense is todah, thanksgiving offered as sacrifice (101), typed as status (102) - a standing offering, a state of grateful worship rather than a momentary act. Uniquely here a source is recorded (103): the God who owns all and needs nothing (v10-12, pair 279514->279499) - the ground of the demand is that God is not hungry for bulls. No organ seats it (104=none); the bearer is the worshipper (105); the operation is to offer (106), targeted to God (107). Manner is none (108) and coupling is none (112) - this thanksgiving stands alone, not welded to another act; intensity, specifier, effect unrecorded (109-111). Nothing is prohibited (113), though the passage sets todah over against empty ritual. The discovery (114) makes the point: because God owns all and is not fed by sacrifice, it is the grateful heart's offering, not slaughtered animals, that honours him. Typed as a characteristic (115), locus God-ward (116 external:god): the inner life's gratitude is here elevated to the true sacrifice - what God actually desires from the human interior.
narratives.story: God speaks and overturns the assumption that he needs the animals brought to his altar - he owns every beast of the forest and would not tell us if he were hungry. What he asks instead is a sacrifice of thanksgiving. The point rests entirely on who God is: since he lacks nothing, the offering that counts is a grateful heart, not a killed bull. This thanksgiving is a standing posture of worship aimed at God, and here it stands on its own as the real thing God wants from a person's inner life.
narratives.variation_note: Distinct within 'thanksgiving' as the one reading with a stated source (God who owns all and needs nothing) and no coupling: todah defined against empty ritual as the sacrifice God actually desires - unlike the paired 'magnify him with thanksgiving' (69:30) or the entry-liturgy of 95:2 / 100:4.

narratives.narrative: Psa 50:23 concludes the same divine speech: 'The one who offers thanksgiving as his sacrifice glorifies me.' The sense is todah offered as sacrifice (101), typed as status (102) - the grateful offering as a standing condition of true worship. Here no source is recorded (103 absent), unlike v14: the ground has already been given earlier in the psalm, so the closing statement simply asserts the outcome. No organ seats it (104=none); the bearer is now 'the true worshipper' (105) - the person defined by this act over against the wicked; the operation is to offer (106), targeted to God (107). Manner is none (108); intensity, specifier, effect unrecorded (109-111). The coupling (112) is a pair 'which glorifies God' (279576->279578) - thanksgiving welded to the honouring of God, its declared consequence-in-worship. Nothing is prohibited (113). The discovery (114) marks this as the psalm's verdict: gratitude is the true sacrifice, honouring God, set against the empty ritual of the wicked. Typed as a characteristic (115), locus God-ward (116 external:god): the inner life's thankfulness is what actually gives God glory.
narratives.story: God's speech ends with a verdict: the person who offers thanksgiving is the one who truly honours him. Thanksgiving here is the mark of the genuine worshipper, over against the hollow religion of the wicked that the psalm has just exposed. It is a settled posture of grateful worship directed at God, and it is bound up with actually glorifying him - the two go together. The whole psalm turns on this: a thankful inner life, not ritual performance, is what gives God glory.
narratives.variation_note: Differs from its twin at 50:14 by dropping the stated source and instead coupling thanksgiving to 'glorifying God': the same todah now cast as the psalm's closing verdict and the badge of the true worshipper against the wicked, rather than the demand grounded in God needing nothing.

narratives.narrative: Psa 52:9 answers the downfall of a boastful, violent man with the psalmist's settled praise: 'I will thank you forever, because you have done it.' The sense is yadah, give thanks/praise, 'I will thank you forever' (101), typed as action (102). No interior source is traced (103 absent) and no organ seats it (104=none). The bearer is the psalmist (105); the operation is to give thanks (106), targeted to God (107). The manner is a pair, 'forever (for what God has done)' (279866->279867) - gratitude for God's decisive act, and unbounded in time (108). Intensity, specifier, effect unrecorded (109-111) - an endpoint without logged gradation. The coupling (112) pairs it with waiting for God's name (279866->279870) - thanks twinned with hope. Nothing is prohibited (113). The discovery (114) reads it as the settled gratitude of the delivered, perpetual thanks for God's judgment and rescue, joined to hopeful waiting. Typed as a characteristic (115), locus God-ward (116 external:god): the inner life, contrasted with the uprooted deceiver of the psalm, comes to rest in enduring, God-directed thanks bound to patient hope.
narratives.story: The psalm has just pictured a powerful liar torn up like an uprooted tree, while the psalmist stands like a flourishing olive in God's house. He responds by promising to thank God forever for what he has done, and to wait on God's good name. The gratitude is unending, fixed on God's decisive act of judgment and rescue, and it comes paired with patient hope. Set against the ruin of the boastful man, the psalmist's inner life settles into lasting, God-directed thanks.
narratives.variation_note: Within 'thank', distinguished by its 'forever' manner and its pairing with waiting/hope: enduring, God-directed gratitude for a completed act of judgment, contrasted with an evildoer's ruin - unlike the felt landing of 7:17 or the crowd-summons of Ps 107.

narratives.narrative: Psa 54:6 vows grateful worship in the middle of danger: 'I will give thanks to your name, O LORD, for it is good.' The sense is yadah (101), typed as action (102). A source is recorded (103): 'because God has delivered him from every trouble (v7) in his faithfulness (v5)' (pair 280009->280015) - the ground of the thanks is God's rescuing faithfulness. No organ seats it (104=none); the bearer is the psalmist (105); the operation is to give thanks (106). The target is a pair, 'your name (for it is good)' (280009->280010) - God's name, qualified as good. The manner is 'with a freewill offering' (280009->280007), and the coupling (112) is that same freewill offering - the thanks enacted in a voluntary gift. Intensity, specifier, effect unrecorded (109-111). Nothing is prohibited (113). The discovery (114) reads it as the grateful response to deliverance, offered freely because God has rescued him from every trouble. Typed as a characteristic (115), locus God-ward (116 external:god): the inner life answers rescue by pouring itself out in willing, God-directed thanks.
narratives.story: Hunted by ruthless strangers who care nothing for God, the psalmist still turns to promise a freewill offering and thanks to God's name because it is good. His gratitude has a clear ground - God's faithfulness has rescued him from every trouble - and it takes shape in a gift given willingly, not under compulsion. The thanks is aimed straight at God, praising his good name. Even mid-danger, his inner life answers deliverance by freely pouring out grateful worship.
narratives.variation_note: Distinct within 'give thanks' by its recorded source (God's rescuing faithfulness) and its enactment 'with a freewill offering': gratitude grounded in a specific deliverance and expressed as a voluntary gift, unlike the sourceless summons-hymns (105:1; 106:1) or the wholehearted resolve of 9:1.

narratives.narrative: Psa 56:12 answers vindicated trust with rendered worship: 'I will render thank offerings to you.' The sense is todah, thank offerings/thanksgiving (101), typed as status (102) - a standing offering owed and paid. No interior source is traced (103 absent) and no organ seats it (104=none). The bearer is the psalmist (105); the operation is to offer/render (106), targeted to God (107). Manner is none (108); intensity, specifier, effect unrecorded (109-111) - an endpoint without logged gradation or consequence. The coupling (112) is a pair, 'the substance of what he renders' (280247->280246) - the vows upon him discharged as thank-offerings. Nothing is prohibited (113). The discovery (114) reads it as the thanksgiving that answers deliverance, the grateful offering of the rescued - gratitude become worship, the fruit of trust vindicated. Typed as a characteristic (115), locus God-ward (116 external:god): the inner life, having trusted God against fear (the psalm's refrain), pays out its gratitude as concrete, God-directed offering.
narratives.story: Afraid but trusting - 'when I am afraid, I put my trust in you' runs through this psalm - the writer ends by declaring that the vows binding him will be paid: he will bring thank-offerings to God. His gratitude is not a mood but something rendered, a debt of thanks discharged in worship. It answers the rescue he trusted God for, and it is directed entirely to God. Trust that held firm in fear now comes out as concrete thanksgiving.

narratives.narrative: Psa 57:9 carries private rescue out to the nations: 'I will give thanks to you, O Lord, among the peoples.' The sense is yadah, 'I will give thanks among the peoples' (101), typed as action (102). A source is recorded (103): 'because God's steadfast love is great to the heavens (v10)' (pair 280439->280356) - the ground is God's boundless love. No organ seats it (104=none); the bearer is the psalmist (105); the operation is to give thanks (106), targeted 'to the Lord, among the peoples' (107). The manner is 'among the peoples/nations' (108) - public, international reach - and the coupling (112) pairs it with singing praises among the nations (280439->280442). Intensity, specifier, effect unrecorded (109-111). Nothing is prohibited (113). The discovery (114) reads it as praise that will not stay private but proclaims God among the peoples, moved by his steadfast love great to the heavens. Typed as a characteristic (115), locus God-ward (116 external:god): sheltering in God 'until the storms pass by,' the inner life answers rescue by projecting its gratitude outward, past itself, to the nations.
narratives.story: Hiding in the shadow of God's wings until disaster passes, the psalmist's heart is 'steadfast,' and he resolves to thank God not in private but out among the nations. His gratitude has a reason - God's love reaches as high as the heavens - and it refuses to stay contained; it goes public, sung among the peoples. The thanks is aimed at God yet broadcast to the whole world. His inner life, rescued, cannot keep its thankfulness to itself.
narratives.variation_note: Within 'give thanks', marked by its outward reach 'among the peoples' and a stated source (God's heaven-high love): gratitude that goes international, paired with public song - like 108:3 but unlike the private wholehearted resolve of 9:1 or 111:1.

narratives.narrative: Psa 69:30 answers deep affliction with a gift greater than any animal: 'I will magnify his name with thanksgiving.' The sense is todah, 'magnify him with thanksgiving' (101), typed as status (102) - a standing grateful offering. No interior source is traced (103 absent) and no organ seats it (104=none). The bearer is the psalmist (105); the operation is to offer (106), targeted to God (107). Manner is none (108); intensity, specifier, effect unrecorded (109-111). The coupling (112) is a pair, 'the substance of the magnifying' (281831->281830) - thanksgiving as the content by which God is exalted, joined to song ('I will praise the name of God with a song'). Nothing is prohibited (113). The discovery (114) reads it as the grateful offering that exalts God, more pleasing to him than ox or bull (v31) - the sacrifice of a grateful heart. Typed as a characteristic (115), locus God-ward (116 external:god): out of drowning distress the inner life brings the one offering that magnifies God - its own thanks - reckoned better than livestock on the altar.
narratives.story: Sunk in mockery and misery, the psalmist promises that he will praise God's name in song and magnify him with thanksgiving - and he adds that this will please God more than an ox or a bull. His gratitude is the very means by which God is made great, welded to his song of praise. It is aimed entirely at God. Even from the depths, his inner life reaches for the offering that counts most: a thankful heart, worth more than any sacrificed animal.
narratives.variation_note: Within 'thanksgiving', distinguished by making thanks the instrument of magnifying God and explicitly ranking it above animal sacrifice: todah as exalting-content out of affliction - unlike the entry-liturgies (95:2; 100:4) or the sourced demand of 50:14.

narratives.narrative: Psa 75:1 opens with a doubled communal thanks: 'We give thanks to you, O God; we give thanks, for your name is near.' The sense is yadah, 'we give thanks to you' (101), typed as action (102). A source is recorded (103): 'because God's name is near (v1)' (pair 282696->282699) - the ground is God's nearness. No organ seats it (104=none); the bearer is plural, the worshippers (105); the operation is to give thanks (106), and the target is a pair, 'to God, whose name is near' (282696->282699). The manner is 'doubled, emphatic' (282696->282698) (108) and the coupling (112) pairs it with the doubled thanks and the recounting of God's wondrous deeds. Intensity, specifier, effect unrecorded (109-111). Nothing is prohibited (113). The discovery (114) reads it as the doubled thanksgiving opening the psalm, the grateful worship of the community moved by God's nearness and his wondrous deeds. Typed as a characteristic (115), locus God-ward (116 external:god): the community's inner life pours out repeated, emphatic thanks because God's name is near.
narratives.story: The community begins by saying it twice over - we give thanks, we give thanks - because God's name is near and his wondrous deeds are told. The repetition is deliberate, a way of underscoring the fullness of their gratitude. The reason is plain: God is close. Their shared inner life answers his nearness with emphatic, God-directed thanks.
narratives.variation_note: The first of the doubled pair at 75:1: carries the stated source (God's name is near) and the target God-whose-name-is-near, whereas its twin (#6) reads the second occurrence purely as emphatic repetition. Together they show gratitude intensified by reiteration.

narratives.narrative: Psa 75:1, second occurrence, is the echo that completes the doubling: 'we give thanks.' The sense is yadah, 'we give thanks, doubled' (101), typed as action (102). Here no source is recorded (103 absent) - unlike its twin (#5), which carried the ground (God's nearness); this second stroke simply repeats, its force lying in reiteration rather than a fresh cause. No organ seats it (104=none); the bearer is the worshippers (105); the operation is to give thanks (106), targeted to God (107). The manner is 'emphatic repetition' (108) and the coupling (112) is a pair naming that emphatic doubling (282698->282696). Intensity, specifier, effect unrecorded (109-111). Nothing is prohibited (113). The discovery (114) reads it as the second of the doubled thanks, yadah repeated for emphasis, the fullness of the community's gratitude to the near God. Typed as a characteristic (115), locus God-ward (116 external:god): the inner life's gratitude registered as sheer repetition - the same thanks said again to mark its fullness.
narratives.story: The second half of the community's doubled opening simply says it again: we give thanks. This time no reason is attached; the point is the repeating itself, a way of showing how full their gratitude is. It is aimed at the God who has drawn near. The inner life underlines its thankfulness by saying the same thing twice.
narratives.variation_note: The echo-half of the 75:1 doubling: drops the source its twin (#5) carried and is read purely as emphatic repetition. The distinction is the finding - gratitude here operates by reiteration, intensity carried by saying it again rather than by a new ground.

narratives.narrative: Psa 79:13 closes a psalm of national devastation with a vow of unending thanks: 'we your people... will give thanks to you forever.' The sense is yadah (101), typed as action (102). No interior source is traced (103 absent) and no organ seats it (104=none). The bearer is corporate, 'we your people' (105) - the flock of God's pasture. The operation is to give thanks (106), targeted 'to God, forever' (107). Manner is none (108); intensity, specifier, effect unrecorded (109-111). The coupling (112) pairs it with recounting his praise 'from generation to generation.' Nothing is prohibited (113). The discovery (114) reads it as the vow of praise closing the lament, gratitude promised across generations even out of desolation. Typed as a characteristic (115), locus God-ward (116 external:god): amid ruined Jerusalem and mocking neighbours, the inner life of the people binds itself to perpetual, God-directed thanks that will be handed on to those who come after.
narratives.story: The psalm has poured out horror - the temple defiled, bodies unburied, the nations jeering - and yet it ends with a promise: we, your people and the sheep of your pasture, will thank you forever and tell your praise to every generation. The gratitude is corporate and unending, and it comes precisely out of desolation, not out of comfort. It is directed wholly at God and meant to be passed down the generations. Even from the wreckage, the people's inner life commits itself to lasting thanks.
narratives.variation_note: Within 'give thanks', distinguished by its corporate bearer ('we your people') and its rise out of national catastrophe: perpetual, generational gratitude vowed from ruin - unlike the festal summons-hymns (105:1; 118:1) or the individual thanks of 111:1.

narratives.narrative: Psa 86:12 gathers the whole self into thanks: 'I give thanks to you, O Lord my God, with my whole heart.' The sense is yadah (101), typed as action (102). No interior source is traced (103 absent) and no organ seats it (104=none) - yet the whole heart is named, meaning not a located organ but the entire inner self. The bearer is the psalmist (105); the operation is to give thanks (106), targeted 'to God wholeheartedly' (107). Manner is none (108); intensity, specifier, effect unrecorded (109-111). The coupling (112) pairs it with the whole heart and with glorifying God's name forever. Nothing is prohibited (113). The discovery (114) reads it as the gratitude of the whole self, thanksgiving vowed forever. Typed as a characteristic (115), locus God-ward (116 external:god): a poor and needy man (the psalm's self-description) answers God's steadfast love by giving thanks with his undivided heart and vowing to glorify God's name without end.
narratives.story: Calling himself poor and needy, the psalmist asks God to teach him an undivided heart to fear his name - and then gives thanks to God with his whole heart, promising to glorify that name forever. The gratitude engages the entire person, nothing split off or withheld, and it is bound to the vow of unending praise. It is aimed wholly at God. His inner life, needy as it is, answers God's great love by turning grateful with all that he is.
narratives.variation_note: Within 'give thanks', marked by wholehearted engagement joined to a 'forever' vow of glorifying God: gratitude of the undivided self from a poor and needy man - close to 111:1 and 138:1 in wholeheartedness, but here welded to unending glorification rather than to public assembly.

narratives.narrative: Psa 92:1 calls thanks the fitting work of the day: 'It is good to give thanks to the LORD.' The sense is yadah (101), typed as action (102). No interior source is traced (103 absent) and no organ seats it (104=none). The bearer is the worshipper (105); the operation is to give thanks (106), targeted 'to the LORD' (107). Manner is none (108); intensity, specifier, effect unrecorded (109-111). The coupling (112) is registered as God-directed (external:god), and its locus (116) is set beside singing praises to God's name - thanks twinned with morning-and-night song. Nothing is prohibited (113). The discovery (114) reads it as the fitting worship that opens the Sabbath song, gratitude as the good work of the day. Typed as a characteristic (115): here thanksgiving is declared simply good and fitting - not commanded by rescue or grief but affirmed as the right and pleasant occupation of the inner life, morning and night.
narratives.story: This Sabbath song opens with a quiet declaration: it is good to give thanks to the LORD, to sing praise to his name, to tell of his love in the morning and his faithfulness at night. Thanks here is not forced out by crisis or triumph; it is simply named as the right and fitting thing to do. It goes hand in hand with song, and it is aimed at God. The inner life finds in daily, unhurried gratitude its proper and good work.
narratives.variation_note: Within 'give thanks', distinctive for framing thanks as intrinsically 'good' and fitting (the Sabbath-song opening) rather than as a response to deliverance or grief: gratitude as the settled, daily good work of the inner life, paired with song.

narratives.narrative: Psa 95:2 makes thanks the manner of approach: 'Let us come into his presence with thanksgiving.' The sense is todah (101), typed here as action (102). No interior source is traced (103 absent) and no organ seats it (104=none). The bearer is plural, the worshippers (105); the operation is to give thanks (106), targeted to God (107). Manner is none as a separate value (108). Intensity, specifier, effect unrecorded (109-111). The coupling (112) is registered as God-directed (external:god), and the locus (116) is set beside coming into his presence - thanksgiving as the mode in which the community draws near. Nothing is prohibited (113). The discovery (114) reads it as the grateful approach, thanks as the manner of coming. Typed as a characteristic (115): here thanksgiving is not the destination but the doorway - the disposition with which the inner life enters God's presence to worship.
narratives.story: The call goes out to come before God with thanksgiving and to shout for joy to the Rock of our salvation. Here gratitude is the way in - the mood and manner in which the worshippers approach God, not a thing done after arriving. It belongs to the whole gathered community and is aimed at God. Their inner life crosses into his presence carried by thanks.
narratives.variation_note: Within 'thanksgiving', distinctive as the manner of approach ('come into his presence with thanksgiving') rather than an offering laid down: todah as the doorway-disposition of entering worship - paired with the gate-entry of 100:4 but distinct from the sacrifice-offerings of 107:22 and 116:17.

narratives.narrative: Psa 97:12 summons the righteous to grateful praise of God's holiness: 'give thanks to his holy name!' The sense is yadah (101), typed as action (102). No interior source is traced (103 absent) and no organ seats it (104=none). The bearer is 'the righteous' (105) - specifically the upright, not worshippers in general. The operation is to give thanks (106), targeted 'to God's holy name' (107) - the object qualified as holy. Manner is none (108); intensity, specifier, effect unrecorded (109-111). The coupling (112) is registered as God-directed (external:god), and the locus (116) is set beside rejoicing ('Rejoice in the LORD, O you righteous'). Nothing is prohibited (113). The discovery (114) reads it as the gratitude of the righteous, praise of God's holiness. Typed as a characteristic (115): as the LORD reigns and light dawns for the upright, the inner life of the righteous responds with joy-joined thanks directed at God's holy name.
narratives.story: As the LORD reigns over all the earth and light is sown for the righteous, the call comes to them: rejoice in the LORD and give thanks to his holy name. The gratitude belongs to the upright in particular, and it rises hand in hand with joy. It is aimed at God's holiness itself. The inner life of the righteous meets God's reign with glad thankfulness.
narratives.variation_note: Within 'give thanks', marked by its bearer (the righteous specifically) and its object (God's holy name), paired with rejoicing: gratitude as the upright's joyful response to God's reign - unlike the corporate festal calls (105:1; 118:1) or the individual wholehearted thanks of 111:1.

narratives.narrative: Psa 100:4 sets thanks at the temple gate: 'Enter... give thanks to him; bless his name!' The sense is yadah (101), typed as action (102). No interior source is traced (103 absent) and no organ seats it (104=none). The bearer is the worshippers (105); the operation is to give thanks (106), targeted to God (107). Manner is none (108); intensity, specifier, effect unrecorded (109-111). The coupling (112) is registered as God-directed (external:god), and the locus (116) is set beside blessing his name. Nothing is prohibited (113). The discovery (114) reads it as the gratitude rendered to God, thanks as the heart of worship. Typed as a characteristic (115): in a psalm calling all the earth to serve God with gladness, the inner life gives thanks as the very substance of entering his courts, joined to blessing his name.
narratives.story: The whole earth is called to worship God with gladness and come into his presence with singing; then, at the gates and courts, to give him thanks and bless his name. Thanks here is the core of what worship is - what you do once you are inside. It goes together with blessing God's name and is aimed at him. The inner life, glad and singing, makes gratitude the heart of its worship.
narratives.variation_note: Within 'give thanks', this is the courts-entry act ('give thanks to him' inside the gates), paired with blessing God's name - closely twinned with the same verse's todah reading (thanksgiv#5, the gate-manner), but here the enacted thanks rendered within, distinct from the manner-of-entry.

narratives.narrative: Psa 100:4 also names thanks as the mode of entry: 'Enter his gates with thanksgiving.' The sense is todah (101), typed as action (102). No interior source is traced (103 absent) and no organ seats it (104=none). The bearer is the worshippers (105); the operation is 'enter with thanksgiving' (106) - the act of entry itself coloured by thanks; the target is 'God's gates' (107). Manner is none (108); intensity, specifier, effect unrecorded (109-111). The coupling (112) is God-directed (external:god), and the locus (116) is set beside praise. Nothing is prohibited (113). The discovery (114) reads it as the grateful approach into God's courts, thanks as the way in. Typed as a characteristic (115): here thanksgiving is the manner of crossing the threshold - the disposition that carries the inner life through the gates - distinct from the thanks-rendered-within of the same verse.
narratives.story: At the temple gates the summons is to enter with thanksgiving and come into the courts with praise. Here thanksgiving is the manner of going in - the grateful spirit in which worshippers cross the threshold. It belongs to the gathered people and moves toward God. Their inner life passes through his gates carried by thanks and praise.
narratives.variation_note: The 100:4 todah (thanksgiving) reading: the manner of entering the gates, whereas the same verse's yadah reading (givethank#11) is the thanks rendered once inside, paired with blessing God's name. The pair distinguishes thanksgiving-as-approach from thanksgiving-as-worship-rendered.

narratives.narrative: Psa 105:1 opens the covenant-hymn with a summons: 'Oh give thanks to the LORD.' The sense is yadah (101), typed as action (102). No interior source is traced (103 absent) and no organ seats it (104=none). The bearer is the worshippers (105); the operation is to give thanks (106), targeted 'to the LORD' (107). Manner is none (108); intensity, specifier, effect unrecorded (109-111). The coupling (112) is God-directed (external:god), and the locus (116) is set beside calling on his name and making known his deeds among the peoples. Nothing is prohibited (113). The discovery (114) reads it as the summons opening the covenant-hymn, gratitude for God's faithfulness across the history of Abraham's seed. Typed as a characteristic (115): the inner life is called to gratitude that overflows into proclamation - thanks joined to calling on God and publishing his works to the nations.
narratives.story: This long hymn of God's faithfulness to Abraham's family opens with a call: give thanks to the LORD, call on his name, make his deeds known among the peoples. Gratitude here is the doorway to proclamation - it does not stop at feeling but spills over into telling others what God has done. It is directed at God. The inner life gives thanks and, in the same breath, publishes God's works to the world.
narratives.variation_note: Within 'give thanks', this is the summons opening a historical covenant-hymn, paired with calling on God's name and proclaiming his deeds to the peoples: gratitude that flows into public proclamation - like 106:1 and 118:1 as festal calls, but tied here to recounting salvation-history.

narratives.narrative: Psa 106:1 frames a national confession of sin with thanks: 'Oh give thanks to the LORD, for he is good; his steadfast love endures forever.' The sense is yadah (101), typed as action (102). No interior source is traced as an inner cause (103 absent), though the reason is stated in the object - God's goodness and enduring love. No organ seats it (104=none). The bearer is the worshippers (105); the operation is to give thanks (106), targeted 'to the LORD' (107). Manner is none (108); intensity, specifier, effect unrecorded (109-111). The coupling (112) is God-directed (external:god), and the locus (116) is set beside praising. Nothing is prohibited (113). The discovery (114) reads it as gratitude for God's enduring love, the frame around the confession that follows. Typed as a characteristic (115): remarkably, the inner life is called to thank God for his goodness precisely as the prelude to a long, unflinching admission of the people's rebellion - gratitude and confession held together.
narratives.story: This psalm is about to recite Israel's long record of rebellion, yet it opens by giving thanks to the LORD because he is good and his love lasts forever. The striking thing is the pairing: gratitude comes first, framing the confession of sin that follows. The thanks is aimed at God and joined to praise. Even as it prepares to admit the worst about the people, their inner life begins by being thankful for God's unchanging goodness.
narratives.variation_note: Within 'give thanks', distinctive for standing as the grateful frame around a confession of national sin: thanks for God's enduring goodness set as prelude to admitting rebellion - the same opening formula as 107:1 and 118:1, but here bracketing failure rather than deliverance or festal joy.

narratives.narrative: Psa 106:47 makes thanks the aim of a plea for gathering: 'save us... that we may give thanks to your holy name.' The sense is yadah (101), typed as action (102). No interior source is traced (103 absent) and no organ seats it (104=none). The bearer is 'the redeemed' (105) - the scattered people longing to be gathered. The operation is to give thanks (106), targeted 'to God's holy name' (107). Manner is none (108); intensity, specifier, effect unrecorded (109-111). The coupling (112) is God-directed (external:god), and the locus (116) is set beside glorying in his praise. Nothing is prohibited (113). The discovery (114) reads it as the vow of the gathered people, the aim of the plea to be saved. Typed as a characteristic (115): here thanksgiving is what salvation is for - the inner life reaches past rescue to the gratitude and triumphant praise that being gathered would make possible.
narratives.story: After the whole sorry history of rebellion, the psalm cries out: save us and gather us from among the nations - so that we may give thanks to your holy name and glory in your praise. Here gratitude is the goal of rescue itself; the people want to be saved precisely so they can be thankful. The thanks is aimed at God's holy name and joined to triumphant praise. Their inner life reaches forward, past the longed-for gathering, to the thanksgiving it would release.
narratives.variation_note: Within 'give thanks', marked as the stated purpose of a plea for salvation ('that we may give thanks'): gratitude as the goal of rescue, borne by the redeemed and joined to glorying in praise - distinct from the opening summons of 106:1 that frames the same psalm.

narratives.narrative: Psa 107:1 opens the great thanksgiving psalm with its keynote: 'Oh give thanks to the LORD, for he is good.' The sense is yadah (101), typed as action (102). No interior source is traced (103 absent) and no organ seats it (104=none). The bearer is 'the redeemed' (105) - those God has gathered from the lands. The operation is to give thanks (106), targeted 'to the LORD' (107). Manner is none (108); intensity, specifier, effect unrecorded (109-111). The coupling (112) is God-directed (external:god), and the locus (116) is set beside the redeemed testifying ('let the redeemed of the LORD say so'). Nothing is prohibited (113). The discovery (114) reads it as the opening call, the frame of the whole thanksgiving. Typed as a characteristic (115): here gratitude is not private but declarative - the inner life of the redeemed is summoned to say so, to voice its thanks aloud as the frame for the four rescue-stories that follow.
narratives.story: This psalm gathers the rescued from every direction and opens with its theme: give thanks to the LORD, for he is good and his love endures forever - let the redeemed say so. Gratitude here is meant to be spoken; the redeemed are not to keep it inside but to declare it. It is aimed at God. Their inner life is called to give voice to its thanks, setting the tone for the rescue-stories that follow.
narratives.variation_note: Within 'give thanks', this is the declarative opening of Ps 107 borne by 'the redeemed' and paired with their testifying ('let the redeemed say so'): gratitude summoned into speech - the frame over the four rescue-refrains (thank#4,#5,#6,#7) that punctuate the same psalm.

narratives.narrative: Psa 107:15 is the refrain answering the freed prisoners' story: 'Let them thank the LORD for his steadfast love.' The sense is yadah, thank (101), typed as action (102). No interior source is traced (103 absent) and no organ seats it (104=none). The bearer is 'the prisoners' (105) - those who sat in darkness and irons, whose bonds God burst. The operation is to thank (106), targeted 'the LORD for his steadfast love' (107). Manner is none (108); intensity, specifier, effect unrecorded (109-111). The coupling (112) is God-directed (external:god), and the locus (116) is set beside his wondrous works (the refrain: 'for his wondrous works to the children of man'). Nothing is prohibited (113). The discovery (114) reads it as the summons to gratitude for the burst bonds. Typed as a characteristic (115): the refrain converts a specific deliverance - prison broken open - into a call for the rescued inner life to answer God's steadfast love with thanks.
narratives.story: Some sat in darkness and iron chains for rebelling against God, until they cried out and he broke their bonds and led them out. To them the refrain calls: let them thank the LORD for his steadfast love and his wonderful works. The gratitude is the fitting answer to a very concrete rescue - prison doors flung open. It is aimed at God's steadfast love. The freed inner life is summoned to turn its release into thanks.
narratives.variation_note: One of the four Ps 107 rescue-refrains: distinguished from its siblings by its bearer - freed prisoners (broken bonds) - and its trigger, deliverance from captivity. Same summons-form as thank#5 (wanderers), thank#6 (the healed), thank#7 (sailors); the varying rescue is the finding.

narratives.narrative: Psa 107:8 is the first refrain, answering the lost wanderers' story: 'Let them thank the LORD for his steadfast love.' The sense is yadah, thank (101), typed as action (102). No interior source is traced (103 absent) and no organ seats it (104=none). The bearer is 'the wanderers' (105) - those who strayed in desert wastes, hungry and thirsty, whom God led by a straight way to a city. The operation is to thank (106), targeted 'the LORD for his steadfast love' (107). Manner is none (108); intensity, specifier, effect unrecorded (109-111). The coupling (112) is God-directed (external:god), and the locus (116) is set beside his wondrous works (the refrain). Nothing is prohibited (113). The discovery (114) reads it as the summons to gratitude, the refrain's response to deliverance. Typed as a characteristic (115): the first strike of the fourfold refrain, calling the rescued inner life - here the lost and famished, now homed - to answer God's steadfast love with thanks.
narratives.story: Some wandered lost in a desert, hungry and thirsty, their spirit fainting, until they cried out and God led them by a straight road to a city where they could live. The refrain answers: let them thank the LORD for his steadfast love and his wonderful works. The gratitude fits a specific rescue - the lost brought home and fed. It is aimed at God's steadfast love. The rescued inner life is called to turn its deliverance into thanks.
narratives.variation_note: The first of the four Ps 107 rescue-refrains: its bearer is the desert wanderers (lost, hungry, then homed). Identical summons-form to thank#4 (prisoners), #6 (healed), #7 (sailors); the difference lies in the distress relieved - here disorientation and hunger.

narratives.narrative: Psa 107:21 is the refrain answering the healed sick: 'Let them thank the LORD for his steadfast love.' The sense is yadah, thank (101), typed as action (102). No interior source is traced (103 absent) and no organ seats it (104=none). The bearer is 'the healed' (105) - fools who through sinful ways drew near death's gates until God sent his word and healed them. The operation is to thank (106), targeted 'the LORD for his steadfast love' (107). Manner is none (108); intensity, specifier, effect unrecorded (109-111). The coupling (112) is God-directed (external:god), and the locus (116) is set beside his wondrous works (the refrain). Nothing is prohibited (113). The discovery (114) reads it as the summons to gratitude for the sent word that healed. Typed as a characteristic (115): the third strike of the refrain, calling the healed inner life - those who neared death through their own folly - to answer God's rescuing word with thanks.
narratives.story: Some were sick to the point of death because of their own foolish, sinful ways, loathing all food, until they cried out and God sent his word and healed them from destruction. The refrain answers: let them thank the LORD for his steadfast love and his wonderful works. The gratitude matches a specific rescue - a deadly illness reversed by God's word. It is aimed at God's steadfast love. The healed inner life is summoned to turn recovery into thanks.
narratives.variation_note: The third of the four Ps 107 rescue-refrains: its bearer is the healed - those brought near death by their own folly. Same summons-form as thank#4, #5, #7; distinctive here is that the sufferers' plight was self-inflicted, and the rescue is God's healing word.

narratives.narrative: Psa 107:22 immediately extends the healed men's refrain into an offering: 'let them offer sacrifices of thanksgiving.' The sense is todah (101), typed as action (102). No interior source is traced (103 absent) and no organ seats it (104=none). The bearer is 'the healed' (105) - the same rescued sufferers. The operation is 'offer thanksgiving' (106), targeted to God (107). Manner is none (108); intensity, specifier, effect unrecorded (109-111). The coupling (112) is God-directed (external:god), and the locus (116) is set beside telling his deeds in songs of joy. Nothing is prohibited (113). The discovery (114) reads it as the thank-offering of the healed, gratitude enacted. Typed as a characteristic (115): where the paired yadah refrain (v21) calls for thanks in words, this todah turns the healed inner life's gratitude into a concrete offering joined to joyful testimony - felt thanks becoming enacted worship.
narratives.story: Right after calling the healed to thank the LORD, the psalm adds: let them offer sacrifices of thanksgiving and tell of his deeds with songs of joy. Here the gratitude is not just spoken but enacted - brought as an offering. It belongs to those God has healed and is aimed at him, joined to glad testimony about what he has done. Their rescued inner life turns thankfulness into concrete worship and song.
narratives.variation_note: Within 'thanksgiving', this is the enacted offering that extends the healed men's spoken refrain (thank#6) at 107:21: todah as sacrifice-and-joyful-testimony, distinct from the entry-manner readings (95:2; 100:4) and paired with telling God's deeds.

narratives.narrative: Psa 107:31 is the fourth refrain, answering the storm-tossed sailors: 'Let them thank the LORD for his steadfast love.' The sense is yadah, thank (101), typed as action (102). No interior source is traced (103 absent) and no organ seats it (104=none). The bearer is 'the sailors' (105) - those who went down to the sea, whom the storm lifted to heaven and dropped to the depths until God stilled the waves. The operation is to thank (106), targeted 'the LORD for his steadfast love' (107). Manner is none (108); intensity, specifier, effect unrecorded (109-111). The coupling (112) is God-directed (external:god), and the locus (116) is set beside his wondrous works (the refrain). Nothing is prohibited (113). The discovery (114) reads it as the summons to gratitude for the calmed storm. Typed as a characteristic (115): the last strike of the fourfold refrain, calling the delivered inner life - sailors brought through terror to their desired haven - to answer God's steadfast love with thanks.
narratives.story: Some went out on ships and met a storm so violent that they were tossed to the sky and plunged to the depths, their courage melting, until they cried out and God hushed the waves and brought them to their desired harbour. The refrain answers: let them thank the LORD for his steadfast love and his wonderful works. The gratitude matches a specific rescue - a deadly storm stilled. It is aimed at God's steadfast love. The delivered inner life is called to turn its safe arrival into thanks.
narratives.variation_note: The fourth of the four Ps 107 rescue-refrains: its bearer is the storm-tossed sailors brought to harbour. Same summons-form as thank#4, #5, #6; the distinctive here is peril at sea calmed by God - the last of the varied deliverances the refrain gathers into thanks.

narratives.narrative: Psa 108:3 carries thanks out to the nations: 'I will give thanks to you, O LORD, among the peoples.' The sense is yadah (101), typed as action (102). No interior source is traced (103 absent) and no organ seats it (104=none). The bearer is the psalmist (105); the operation is to give thanks (106), targeted 'to God among the peoples' (107). Manner is none as a separate value (108); intensity, specifier, effect unrecorded (109-111). The coupling (112) is God-directed (external:god), and the locus (116) is set beside singing praises among the nations. Nothing is prohibited (113). The discovery (114) reads it as the public thanksgiving, praise carried to the nations. Typed as a characteristic (115): with a steadfast heart the inner life resolves to thank God not privately but openly among the peoples, joined to song - gratitude that refuses to stay contained.
narratives.story: 'My heart is steadfast, O God,' the psalmist says, and he wakes the dawn with music, resolving to thank God among the peoples and sing his praise among the nations. His gratitude is deliberately public, carried out beyond himself to the wider world, and it goes hand in hand with song. It is aimed at God. His settled inner life turns its thankfulness into open, international praise.
narratives.variation_note: Within 'give thanks', this shares the outward reach 'among the peoples' with 57:9 (borrowed language) but, unlike 57:9, records no stated source - here the thanks flows from a steadfast heart declared, gratitude broadcast to the nations and paired with song.

narratives.narrative: Psa 109:30 turns a psalm of bitter complaint toward loud thanks: 'With my mouth I will give great thanks to the LORD.' The sense is yadah, thanks (101), typed as action (102). No interior source is traced (103 absent) and no organ seats it (104=none) - though 'with my mouth' names the instrument of voicing, not a seat. The bearer is the psalmist (105); the operation is 'give great thanks' (106) - thanks intensified within the operation itself; the target is 'to the LORD' (107). Manner is none as a separate value (108); intensity, specifier, effect unrecorded as their own rows (109-111), yet 'great' inside the operation signals a heightened measure. The coupling (112) is God-directed (external:god), and the locus (116) is set beside praising in the throng ('in the midst of the throng I will praise him'). Nothing is prohibited (113). The discovery (114) reads it as the vow of thanksgiving, the lament turning to praise. Typed as a characteristic (115): assailed by cursing enemies, the inner life pivots from complaint to a vow of loud, public, God-directed thanks.
narratives.story: This psalm is heavy with grievance against lying, cursing enemies, yet near its end the psalmist turns: with his mouth he will give great thanks to the LORD and praise him amid the crowd. The gratitude is loud and public, spoken aloud in the throng, and it is emphatically full - great thanks, not muted. It is aimed at God. Out of a heart weighed down by attack, his inner life swings around into vocal, wholehearted thanksgiving.
narratives.variation_note: Within 'thank', distinctive for its heightened measure ('great thanks') carried inside the operation and its public, voiced setting ('with my mouth,' 'in the throng'): gratitude as a lament's pivot to loud praise - unlike the quiet landing of 7:17 or the summons-refrains of Ps 107.

narratives.narrative: Psa 111:1 opens an alphabetic praise-psalm with wholehearted thanks: 'I will give thanks to the LORD with my whole heart.' The sense is yadah (101), typed as action (102). No interior source is traced (103 absent) and no organ seats it (104=none) - the whole heart is the entire inner self, not a located organ. The bearer is the psalmist (105); the operation is to give thanks (106), targeted 'to the LORD with the whole heart' (107). Manner is none (108); intensity, specifier, effect unrecorded (109-111). The coupling (112) is God-directed (external:god), and the locus (116) is set beside the whole heart and the company of the upright ('in the company of the upright, in the congregation'). Nothing is prohibited (113). The discovery (114) reads it as undivided gratitude, thanks from the entire inner self. Typed as a characteristic (115): the inner life gives itself wholly to thanks, and does so in the assembly of the upright - private wholeheartedness voiced in public company.
narratives.story: This psalm opens with a resolve to thank the LORD with the whole heart, in the gathering of the upright. What marks it is completeness - the entire inner self is given over, nothing divided or withheld - and setting, for the private thanks is offered openly among the godly. It is aimed at God. Here the inner life pours out undivided gratitude in the company of others who share it.
narratives.variation_note: Within 'give thanks', shares wholehearted engagement with 9:1, 86:12 and 138:1 but distinctively sets that undivided thanks 'in the company of the upright, in the congregation': private wholeness voiced in public assembly, opening an alphabetic praise-psalm.

narratives.narrative: Psa 116:17 answers deliverance from death with an enacted offering: 'I will offer to you the sacrifice of thanksgiving.' The sense is todah (101), typed as action (102). No interior source is traced (103 absent) and no organ seats it (104=none). The bearer is the psalmist (105); the operation is 'offer thanksgiving' (106), targeted to God (107). Manner is none (108); intensity, specifier, effect unrecorded (109-111). The coupling (112) is God-directed (external:god), and the locus (116) is set beside calling on God's name ('and call on the name of the LORD'). Nothing is prohibited (113). The discovery (114) reads it as the thank-offering of the delivered, gratitude enacted. Typed as a characteristic (115): having been snatched from death (the psalm's theme, 'you have delivered my soul from death'), the inner life pays its vows to God with a concrete thank-offering joined to calling on his name - felt rescue turned into enacted worship.
narratives.story: Rescued from death, tears, and stumbling, the psalmist asks what he can give back to God, and answers by lifting the cup of salvation, offering a sacrifice of thanksgiving, and calling on the LORD's name. His gratitude is not merely felt but brought - an offering laid down. It answers a rescue from the grave itself and is aimed at God, joined to prayer. His delivered inner life turns its thankfulness into concrete worship.
narratives.variation_note: Within 'thanksgiving', this is the enacted sacrifice of the death-delivered, paired with calling on God's name and paying vows - distinct from the entry-manner readings (95:2; 100:4) and the sourced demand of 50:14, and sharing enacted-offering ground with 107:22.

narratives.narrative: Psa 118:1 opens the processional psalm with its antiphonal keynote: 'Oh give thanks to the LORD, for he is good; his steadfast love endures forever.' The sense is yadah (101), typed as action (102). No interior source is traced as an inner cause (103 absent) - the reason lodges in the object, God's goodness and enduring love. No organ seats it (104=none). The bearer is the worshippers (105); the operation is to give thanks (106), targeted 'to the LORD' (107). Manner is none (108); intensity, specifier, effect unrecorded (109-111). The coupling (112) is God-directed (external:god), and the locus (116) is set beside his enduring steadfast love (the refrain answered by Israel, Aaron's house, and those who fear the LORD). Nothing is prohibited (113). The discovery (114) reads it as the antiphonal call opening the psalm. Typed as a characteristic (115): the inner life's gratitude is voiced as a shared, responsive summons - one voice calling, the assembly answering - founded on God's everlasting love. This same call closes the psalm at v29, where it recurs.
narratives.story: This festival psalm opens and closes with the same great refrain: give thanks to the LORD, for he is good, his love endures forever - a call taken up in turn by all Israel, the priests, and all who fear God. Gratitude here is a shared, answering thing, one voice leading and the crowd responding. Its ground is God's unending goodness. The whole worshipping community's inner life is drawn into thanks, and the psalm bookends itself with this call, sounding it again at its very end.
narratives.variation_note: Within 'give thanks', this is the antiphonal opening (and, at v29, closing) call of the processional Ps 118: shared responsive gratitude grounded in God's enduring love - the same formula as 106:1 and 107:1, but here framing a liturgy of communal response. Recurs at v29.

narratives.narrative: Psa 118:19 makes thanks the purpose of entering the temple: 'Open to me the gates of righteousness... that I may enter through them and give thanks to the LORD.' The sense is yadah (101), typed as action (102). No interior source is traced (103 absent) and no organ seats it (104=none). The bearer is the psalmist (105); the operation is to give thanks (106), targeted 'to the LORD on entering' (107). Manner is none (108); intensity, specifier, effect unrecorded (109-111). The coupling (112) is God-directed (external:god), and the locus (116) is set beside entering the gates of righteousness. Nothing is prohibited (113). The discovery (114) reads it as the thanksgiving that is the aim of entering the gates. Typed as a characteristic (115): here gratitude is the goal of approach - the inner life asks for the gates to be opened precisely so that it may go in and give thanks, thanksgiving as the reason for entering God's presence.
narratives.story: The psalmist calls for the gates of righteousness to be opened so that he can go through them and give thanks to the LORD. Here gratitude is the very reason for entering - he wants the doors opened so he can get inside and be thankful. The thanks is aimed at God. His inner life presses toward the sanctuary with thanksgiving as its whole purpose.
narratives.variation_note: Within 'give thanks', distinctive as the stated aim of entering the temple gates ('that I may enter... and give thanks'): gratitude as the goal of approach - contrast the same psalm's opening antiphonal summons (118:1) and the personal answered-thanks of 118:21.

narratives.narrative: Psa 118:21 gives the personal ground of the temple thanks: 'I thank you that you have answered me and have become my salvation.' The sense is yadah, thank (101), typed as action (102). No interior source is traced (103 absent) and no organ seats it (104=none). The bearer is the psalmist (105); the operation is to thank (106), targeted 'God for answering' (107) - thanks tied to a specific answered prayer. Manner is none (108); intensity, specifier, effect unrecorded (109-111). The coupling (112) is God-directed (external:god), and the locus (116) is set beside God's answer and salvation. Nothing is prohibited (113). The discovery (114) reads it as the personal thanks for the deliverance. Typed as a characteristic (115): where v19 sought entry in order to thank, here the inner life gives the reason - God answered and became his salvation. This is gratitude grounded in a concrete, answered cry.
narratives.story: Once inside, the psalmist gives his reason for thanks: I thank you because you answered me and became my salvation. The gratitude is deeply personal and pinned to a specific event - a prayer heard, a rescue given. It is aimed directly at God. His inner life responds to being answered by turning to thank the one who saved him.
narratives.variation_note: Within 'thank', this is the personal, grounded thanks of Ps 118 ('you have answered me and become my salvation') - the reason behind the entry-thanks of 118:19, and distinct from the psalm's corporate opening summons (118:1).

narratives.narrative: Psa 118:28 makes thanks the confession of belonging: 'You are my God, and I will give thanks to you.' The sense is yadah (101), typed as action (102). No interior source is traced (103 absent) and no organ seats it (104=none). The bearer is the psalmist (105); the operation is to give thanks (106), targeted to God (107). Manner is none (108); intensity, specifier, effect unrecorded (109-111). The coupling (112) is God-directed (external:god), and the locus (116) is set beside extolling him ('I will extol you'). Nothing is prohibited (113). The discovery (114) reads it as the personal thanksgiving to God as his own. Typed as a characteristic (115): gratitude here rests on relationship - 'you are my God' - the inner life claiming God as its own and answering that bond with thanks joined to exaltation.
narratives.story: Near the close of this festival psalm the worshipper declares: you are my God, and I will give you thanks; you are my God, I will exalt you. The gratitude flows out of belonging - because God is his own God, he turns to thank and lift him high. It is aimed directly at God. His inner life owns its relationship with God and answers it with thanks and praise.
narratives.variation_note: Within 'give thanks', distinctive for grounding thanks in personal relationship ('You are my God'): gratitude as the answer of belonging, paired with exalting God - close to the psalm's frame (118:1) yet intimate and possessive rather than corporate-antiphonal.

narratives.narrative: Psa 122:4 names thanks as the purpose of pilgrimage: the tribes 'go up... to give thanks to the name of the LORD.' The sense is yadah (101), typed as action (102). No interior source is traced (103 absent) and no organ seats it (104=none). The bearer is corporate, 'the tribes' (105) - all Israel gathered. The operation is to give thanks (106), targeted 'to the name of the LORD' (107). Manner is none (108); intensity, specifier, effect unrecorded (109-111). The coupling (112) is God-directed (external:god), and the locus (116) is set beside the tribes going up to Jerusalem. Nothing is prohibited (113). The discovery (114) reads it as the thanksgiving that is the aim of the pilgrimage, the tribes gathered to praise God's name. Typed as a characteristic (115): here gratitude is what the whole nation journeys for - the collective inner life converges on Jerusalem so that it may give thanks to God's name, thanksgiving as the destination of pilgrimage.
narratives.story: Glad to go up to the house of the LORD, the psalmist recalls that this is where the tribes go - by an ordinance for Israel - to give thanks to the name of the LORD. Gratitude here is the reason a whole nation makes the journey; the pilgrimage exists so the people can be thankful together. It is aimed at God's name. The shared inner life of all the tribes converges on Jerusalem for the sake of thanks.
narratives.variation_note: Within 'give thanks', distinctive for its corporate bearer (the tribes of Israel) and its framing as the goal of pilgrimage to Jerusalem: national gratitude as the appointed purpose of going up - unlike individual thanks (111:1; 118:21) or the festal summons-hymns.

narratives.narrative: Psa 136:1 opens the great litany with its refrain-launching call: 'Give thanks to the LORD, for he is good, for his steadfast love endures forever.' The sense is yadah (101), typed as action (102). No interior source is traced as an inner cause (103 absent) - the ground is stated in the refrain, God's enduring love. No organ seats it (104=none). The bearer is the worshippers (105); the operation is to give thanks (106), targeted to God (107). Manner is none (108); intensity, specifier, effect unrecorded (109-111). The coupling (112) is God-directed (external:god), and the locus (116) is set beside the antiphonal refrain of steadfast love that answers every line. Nothing is prohibited (113). The discovery (114) reads it as the opening imperative of the litany, thanks for God's enduring love. Typed as a characteristic (115): the inner life is summoned to a relentless, responsive gratitude - each act of God met by the same answer, 'his steadfast love endures forever.' This same call recurs at v2, v3 (give thanks to the God of gods, the Lord of lords) and v26 (give thanks to the God of heaven).
narratives.story: This psalm is one long litany where every single line is answered by the same refrain: his steadfast love endures forever. It opens by calling the worshippers to give thanks to the LORD because he is good, and it keeps repeating that call - to the God of gods, the Lord of lords, and finally the God of heaven. Gratitude here is relentless and responsive, met at every turn by the assurance of God's unfailing love. The community's inner life is swept up into thanks that answers back to each of God's deeds.
narratives.variation_note: Within 'give thanks', this launches the antiphonal litany of Ps 136 and recurs across it (v2, v3, v26): gratitude as a relentless, repeated call answered by the fixed refrain of steadfast love - the most sustained corporate summons among these readings. Recurs at 136:2, 136:3, 136:26.

narratives.narrative: Psa 138:1 opens with defiant wholehearted thanks: 'I give you thanks, O LORD, with my whole heart; before the gods I sing your praise.' The sense is yadah (101), typed as action (102). No interior source is traced (103 absent) and no organ seats it (104=none) - the whole heart is the entire inner self, not a located organ. The bearer is the psalmist (105); the operation is to give thanks (106), targeted 'to God with the whole heart' (107). Manner is none (108); intensity, specifier, effect unrecorded (109-111). The coupling (112) is God-directed (external:god), and the locus (116) is set beside the whole heart and singing ('before the gods I sing your praise'). Nothing is prohibited (113). The discovery (114) reads it as undivided thanksgiving, gratitude from the entire self. Typed as a characteristic (115): the inner life gives itself wholly to thanks and does so boldly 'before the gods' - undivided gratitude voiced in the face of every rival power.
narratives.story: The psalmist opens by thanking God with his whole heart and singing his praise defiantly before the gods - the rival powers of the nations. The gratitude engages his entire self, nothing held back, and it is bold, sounded out in the presence of every competitor to God. It is aimed at God alone. His undivided inner life turns thankful and unashamed, praising God over against all pretenders.
narratives.variation_note: The 'give you thanks' item's first reading: individual, wholehearted gratitude voiced defiantly 'before the gods' - distinct from its second reading (138:4), where the same word is borne by the kings of the earth. Bearer and setting differ; here it is the single worshipper's bold, undivided thanks.

narratives.narrative: Psa 138:2 directs thanks to God's name for his love and truth: 'and give thanks to your name for your steadfast love and your faithfulness.' The sense is yadah (101), typed as action (102). No interior source is traced (103 absent) and no organ seats it (104=none). The bearer is the psalmist (105); the operation is to give thanks (106), targeted 'to God's name' (107). Manner is none (108); intensity, specifier, effect unrecorded (109-111). The coupling (112) is God-directed (external:god), and the locus (116) is set beside bowing down ('I bow down toward your holy temple'). Nothing is prohibited (113). The discovery (114) reads it as thanks directed to God's name for his love and truth. Typed as a characteristic (115): the inner life's gratitude is here bodily and reverent - bowing toward the temple - and specified in its object: God's steadfast love and faithfulness, the very qualities for which thanks is given.
narratives.story: Bowing toward God's holy temple, the psalmist gives thanks to God's name for his steadfast love and his faithfulness. The gratitude names exactly what it is thankful for - God's unfailing love and his reliability - and it comes with a posture of reverence, a bowing down. It is aimed at God's name. His inner life turns grateful and humble, honouring the God who is both loving and true.
narratives.variation_note: Within 'give thanks', this specifies the ground in the object - God's steadfast love and faithfulness - and pairs thanks with a reverent bowing: gratitude directed and humble, distinct from the wholehearted opening of the same psalm (giveyouthank#1) and its universal-kings reading (giveyouthank#2).

narratives.narrative: Psa 138:4 widens thanks to the whole earth's rulers: 'All the kings of the earth shall give you thanks, O LORD.' The sense is yadah (101), typed as action (102). No interior source is traced (103 absent) and no organ seats it (104=none). The bearer is not the psalmist but 'the kings of the earth' (105) - a projected, universal company. The operation is to give thanks (106), targeted to God (107). Manner is none (108); intensity, specifier, effect unrecorded (109-111). The coupling (112) is God-directed (external:god), and the locus (116) is set beside hearing his words ('for they have heard the words of your mouth'). Nothing is prohibited (113). The discovery (114) reads it as the future homage of kings, thanks that will spread to the powers of the earth. Typed as a characteristic (115): here gratitude is projected outward and forward - the inner life foresees even the world's rulers turning thankful once they hear God's words, thanksgiving as a coming, universal response.
narratives.story: The psalmist looks ahead and declares that all the kings of the earth will one day thank God, once they have heard the words of his mouth. The gratitude here is not his own but foreseen in others - the mightiest rulers of the world turning thankful. It is aimed at God. His inner life reaches beyond itself to imagine a day when thanks to God spreads to every throne on earth.
narratives.variation_note: The 'give you thanks' item's second reading: its bearer is the kings of the earth, a projected universal homage, whereas its first reading (138:1) is the psalmist's own wholehearted, defiant thanks. Individual present gratitude versus foreseen worldwide thanks - the shift in bearer and horizon is the finding.

narratives.narrative: Psa 140:13 closes a psalm of deadly danger with the gratitude of the vindicated: 'the righteous shall give thanks to your name.' The sense is 'give thanks (upright)' (101), typed as affect (102) - felt gratitude, not merely an enacted rite. No interior source is traced (103 absent) and no organ seats it (104=none). The bearer is 'the upright' (105); the operation (106) is the righteous responding to vindication with thanksgiving and dwelling in God's presence - a two-part landing. Its target is 'grateful-response' (107) - the interior's own answering gratitude - and it is coupled as 'thank-and-dwell' (112), thanks welded to abiding before God's face. Manner is none (108); intensity, specifier, effect unrecorded (109-111). Nothing is prohibited (113). The discovery (114) reads it as the arc closing in gratitude, the interior moving from threat through assurance to thanks. Typed as a characteristic (115), located internally as an ib-state (116): the inner life, hunted through the psalm, comes finally to rest in felt gratitude and settled dwelling with God.
narratives.story: This psalm has begged rescue from violent men who plan to trip up the psalmist's feet, and it ends in confidence: surely the righteous will give thanks to God's name and the upright will dwell in his presence. The gratitude is a felt thing, and it arrives as the resolution of the whole ordeal - the inner life travelling from threat, through assurance, into thanks. It comes joined to a settled abiding before God. The hunted inner life finds its resting-place in grateful nearness to God.
narratives.variation_note: Within 'give thanks', distinctive for its internal locus and 'affect' typing (like the ib-state readings 9:1, 145:10): felt gratitude as the arc-closing landing of a persecution psalm, welded to dwelling in God's presence - not the God-directed public act that dominates this item elsewhere.

narratives.narrative: Psa 142:7 reaches past rescue to thanks before it arrives: 'Bring my soul out of prison, that I may give thanks to your name.' The sense is 'anticipated thanksgiving' (101), typed as affect (102) - gratitude felt in advance, in hope. No interior source is traced (103 absent) and no organ seats it (104=none). The bearer is the psalmist (105); the operation (106) is the self already reaching past rescue to thanks - gratitude anticipated among the righteous who will gather round him. Its target is 'hope-in-thanks' (107) - thanksgiving held as forward-leaning hope - and it is coupled as 'thank-when-freed' (112), thanks contingent on the longed-for release. Manner is none (108); intensity, specifier, effect unrecorded (109-111). Nothing is prohibited (113). The discovery (114) reads it as the interior leaning forward into future praise, gratitude pre-formed in hope. Typed as a characteristic (115), located internally as an ib-state (116): from the depths of a cave (the psalm's setting), with no one caring for his soul, the inner life pre-forms its gratitude, thanksgiving reaching ahead of the deliverance it still awaits.
narratives.story: Alone in a cave, feeling that no one cares whether he lives or dies, the psalmist prays to be brought out of his prison so that he can give thanks to God's name, with the righteous gathering around him. What is striking is that his gratitude runs ahead of the rescue - he is already thankful in hope, before he is freed. It is the felt reaching-forward of a trapped inner life toward the praise it longs to give. From his lowest point, his inner life leans into a thanksgiving not yet possible.

narratives.narrative: Psa 145:10 turns thanks into the whole creation's and community's response: 'All your works shall give thanks to you, O LORD, and your saints shall bless you.' The sense is 'the saints give thanks' (101), typed as affect (102) - felt, willing gratitude. No interior source is traced (103 absent) and no organ seats it (104=none). The bearer is 'the saints' (105) - the godly community (alongside all God's works). The operation (106) is that all God's works give thanks and his saints bless him - the community's gratitude gathered into a chorus. Its target is 'corporate-thanks' (107) and it is coupled as 'saints-give-thanks' (112). Manner is none (108); intensity, specifier, effect unrecorded (109-111). Nothing is prohibited (113). The discovery (114) reads it as the interior of the whole godly community turning grateful. Typed as a characteristic (115), located internally as an ib-state (116): here the inner life is not one person's but a shared, corporate state - the collective interior of the faithful turned toward thanks, echoing the praise of all created things.
narratives.story: In this hymn to God's greatness, everything God has made is said to give him thanks, and his faithful people bless him. The gratitude here is shared and communal - not one voice but the whole company of the godly, joined even by all creation. It is a felt, willing turning of the community's heart toward thanks. Together, the inner life of God's people becomes grateful, taking up the praise that all God's works already offer.
narratives.variation_note: Within 'give thanks', distinctive for its corporate, internal locus (an ib-state, like 9:1, 140:13): the shared gratitude of the whole godly community and all creation - felt corporate thanks, not the individual act or the God-directed public summons that mark this item elsewhere.
